headline: A documented `schemeAllowlist` that no code read is gone, and two checks hold the reference pages to what the code does
summary: `b.guardMarkdown.validate` documented an option that existed only on its documentation line. Setting it did nothing, and the default it quoted described a constant on a different code path. The line is removed, and a check now compares every documented option against the code that would read it. A second check holds the reference pages to American English.

items.title: `b.guardMarkdown.validate` no longer documents an option nothing reads
items.body:
The option block for `b.guardMarkdown.validate` listed `schemeAllowlist: string[]` with a default of `["http","https","mailto"]`. That name appeared once in the whole framework, on that line. No code read it, so an operator passing `{ schemeAllowlist: ["https"] }` to stop `http:` link targets changed nothing and got no error, and the quoted default described a constant used by `b.guardMarkdown.render` rather than by `validate`.

The line is removed. `validate` screens schemes against a fixed dangerous-scheme list under `dangerousSchemePolicy`, `imageSchemePolicy`, `autolinkSchemePolicy` and `referenceLinkPolicy`, which are documented and implemented. `b.guardMarkdown.render` limits link targets to `http`, `https`, `mailto` and relative references, which its own page already states.

Nothing to change on upgrade: the option never had an effect, so no configuration depended on it. An operator who set it expecting narrower schemes was not getting them and should use the scheme policies above.

items.title: `b.auth.oauth.parseJarmResponse` documents the options it accepts
items.body:
The page listed `acceptedAlgs` and `maxClockSkewMs`. Neither reaches the JWT verification: the JARM response's signature is checked with a fixed set of options, and neither name appears anywhere in the framework's code. An operator narrowing the algorithms a JARM response may be signed with, or tightening the clock skew, got a silent no-op, which on an authorization-response verifier is a false sense of a tightened boundary.

Both are removed. The page now lists `requireIssParam`, which the function does accept and forward, and which it had not documented.

If you were passing either removed option, verification was already running with the framework's own algorithm set and skew; nothing about how a response is verified changes here, only what the page claims.

items.title: Two pages no longer document a positional argument as an option
items.body:
`b.mail.bimi.validateTinyPsSvg` carried an option block listing `svgBytes: Buffer | string`, and `b.consent.recognizedPurpose` one listing `name: string`. Both take that value as their first positional argument, which their signature lines already show, and `recognizedPurpose`'s own example calls it as `b.consent.recognizedPurpose("educational-only")`. Following the option block instead gave `validateTinyPsSvg({ svgBytes: buf })`, an object that is neither a Buffer nor a string.

Both option blocks are removed. Pass the value directly.

items.title: A documented option must appear in the code
items.body:
Every option named in a reference page's option block is now compared against the framework's own source, and a name that appears nowhere in the code fails the build. An option is often handed to a helper in another file, so the check reads the whole tree rather than the declaring file.

It does not try to decide whether the code honors an option, which is a data-flow question a text search cannot settle: options are consumed here through profile, mapping and rule tables as often as through a direct property read. It settles the narrower question exactly, which is whether the name exists in the code at all.

The existing sibling check reads the option allowlist the code states. This one reads the option block the documentation states, and the two are separate routes to advertised surface: an option can be documented without appearing in an allowlist, which is how this one survived.

items.title: An option block belongs to a primitive that takes an options object
items.body: A block whose single documented key is also the primitive's single parameter now fails the build. Documenting the fields of an object argument is the convention and stays correct however that argument is named, so a page listing what an audit event carries is unaffected; the defect is a page that presents the argument itself as a field of an options object.

items.title: Reference-page prose is American English
items.body:
Every documentation block in the framework's source becomes a reference page, so 36 lines reading `behaviour`, `honours`, `recognise`, `normalises`, `defence` and `catalogue` are corrected. A check holds the rest.

Two kinds of text keep their source spelling and are listed in the check with the reason: an identifier or API value, since `dual.grant.cancelled` is an emitted event name and the `cancelled` data-subject-request status is part of a documented union, and a standard's own wording, since ISO 18013-5 names the credential a mobile driving licence and the EU AI Act Art. 50(3) notice text is quoted verbatim.

items.title: A live rate-limit check stops racing a window boundary
items.body:
The cluster rate-limiter's window is aligned to the epoch, so a one-minute window puts a boundary on every wall-clock minute. The MySQL and Postgres checks took four counted requests in sequence against a real database and asserted the fourth was refused; a sequence that straddled a boundary saw the counter reset and the fourth allowed, failing a check whose subject was the SQL upsert rather than wall-clock timing.

Each sequence now reads the window on both sides of itself and runs again on a fresh key when it turned over, so a boundary costs a repeat rather than a failure. Both still exercise the window-rollover branch by advancing the stored window directly. Repository tooling only; the limiter is unchanged.

items.title: A growth measurement holds up on a loaded machine
items.body: The check that the growth helper separates a linear curve from a quadratic one measured its baseline at 25ms. Scheduler delay adds a fixed amount to both readings, and against a 25ms denominator that was enough to pull a true ratio of 16 below the threshold, so the check failed on a busy machine while nothing it tests was wrong. The baseline is 50ms now, which takes the tolerated delay from about 22ms to about 44ms. Repository tooling only.

items.title: Reference-page wording
items.body: Numeric ranges in the CBOR, PIPL and redirect pages read `28 to 30` rather than using a dash. Sentences in `b.money`, `b.apiKey`, `b.audit`, `b.codepointClass`, `b.logStream`, `b.queue` and `b.auditSign` that carried an aside on a dash, or stated a result as what it costs or buys, now name what happens and to what. No documented behavior changes.
